These optional projects let you put your NumPy skills into practice and earn extra credit. They work exactly like the side projects of Module 2: the submission format, the extra credit, and the guidance on using AI tools are described on the [Module 2 Side Projects page](../structures/side_projects.qmd). Only three side projects in total count towards the bonus, so you can mix projects from both modules.

## Numerical Linear Algebra

Implement four classic algorithms using only NumPy: centering a matrix, the Gram-Schmidt process, the conjugate gradient method, and the power method. Each is a short recipe, but together they show how much of linear algebra reduces to dot products and matrix-vector products.

Main concepts: broadcasting, `axis`, dot products, norms, and iterative algorithms.

[Numerical Linear Algebra](sp_numerical_linear_algebra.qmd){.btn .btn-secondary}

## MNIST Digit Recognition

Build your first "AI model": a classifier that recognizes handwritten digits by comparing each drawing with the average look of every digit. You will measure its accuracy on real data and discover where such a simple idea breaks down.

Main concepts: image arrays, boolean masks, array arithmetic, distances, and accuracy.

[MNIST Digit Recognition](sp_mnist.qmd){.btn .btn-secondary}

## Snell's Law

Estimate the refractive index of an unknown material from measured angles of incidence and refraction. You will use vectorized trigonometry and descriptive statistics to turn noisy measurements into a single estimate.

Main concepts: two-dimensional slicing, vectorized trigonometric functions, and descriptive statistics.

[Snell's Law](sp_snell.qmd){.btn .btn-secondary}
